slides.title: What Is a Leader?
slides.text: A leader helps a group get things done. Showing a friend a game's rules is one way to lead.

widgetConfig.scenario: During a group game, one kid helps everyone understand the rules and makes sure everyone gets a turn. What are they doing?

options.label: Being a leader — helping the group and making things fair
options.outcome: Exactly! A leader helps others and makes sure things are fair, not just gives orders.

options.label: Being bossy
options.outcome: Helping others and being fair is leadership, not bossiness — bossy means ordering people around without caring about them.

options.label: Just playing the game normally
options.outcome: Helping everyone and keeping things fair is actually a leadership role, even during a game!

slides.title: Leading by Example
slides.text: A good leader shows how, not just tells. Cleaning up first makes friends want to help too.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want your friends to help clean up after playing. What's a leader-like way to encourage that?

options.label: Start cleaning up yourself first
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader shows how, not just tells — cleaning up first makes friends more likely to join in.

options.label: Just order everyone else to do it while you don't help
options.outcome: Ordering others without helping yourself doesn't show real leadership — leading by example works better.

options.label: Wait for someone else to start first
options.outcome: Waiting for someone else misses the chance to lead — starting yourself sets the example.

slides.title: Being a Good Sport
slides.text: A good leader plays fair and stays kind. Saying "good game" is kind, even if you lose.

widgetConfig.scenario: You just lost a game to a friend. What's the best way to react?

options.label: Say "Good game!" and mean it
options.outcome: That's being a great sport! Congratulating others, even when you lose, shows real leadership.

options.label: Say the game wasn't fair
options.outcome: Blaming the game when you lose can hurt your friendship. A good sport accepts the result graciously.

options.label: Refuse to play with them again
options.outcome: Walking away upset can make others not want to play with you. Good sports keep playing and try again.

slides.title: Saying Sorry
slides.text: Good leaders say sorry when they make a mistake. Saying sorry helps friends trust you more.

widgetConfig.scenario: You accidentally knock over your friend's blocks. What does a good leader do?

options.label: Say sorry
options.outcome: Exactly right! Good leaders say sorry when they make a mistake — it helps friends trust you.

options.label: Blame someone else
options.outcome: Blaming someone else for your own mistake isn't honest leadership — saying sorry is the right move.

options.label: Walk away and say nothing
options.outcome: Walking away without saying anything doesn't fix things — saying sorry shows you care.

slides.title: Helping Without Being Asked
slides.text: Good leaders help even when no one asks. Picking up a dropped toy is a kind, helpful act.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT an example of helping without being asked?

items.label: Waiting to be asked before ever helping
Offering to share without being asked

widgetConfig.explanation: Waiting to be asked is the opposite of helping without being asked — the other three are all examples of noticing and helping on your own.

slides.title: Cheering Others On
slides.text: Cheering for a friend helps them feel brave. Clapping for someone trying something hard is kind.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend is trying something hard and nervous about it. What's a good leader thing to do?

options.label: Clap and cheer for them
options.outcome: Exactly right! Cheering for a friend helps them feel brave — clapping for someone trying something hard is kind.

options.label: Laugh at them if they fail
options.outcome: Laughing at someone trying their best isn't kind — cheering them on helps them feel brave instead.

options.label: Ignore them completely
options.outcome: Ignoring them misses a chance to help them feel brave — cheering them on is much kinder.

slides.title: Staying Calm
slides.text: Good leaders stay calm when things go wrong. Taking a deep breath helps you think of what to do next.

widgetConfig.scenario: Something goes wrong with your group's plan. What should a good leader do?

options.label: Stay calm and take a deep breath
options.outcome: Exactly right! Good leaders stay calm when things go wrong — taking a deep breath helps you think of what to do next.

options.label: Panic and yell
options.outcome: Panicking and yelling doesn't help solve the problem — staying calm helps you think more clearly.

options.label: Give up immediately
options.outcome: Giving up doesn't fix what went wrong — staying calm and thinking it through works much better.

slides.title: Trying Again
slides.text: A block tower can fall down. A good leader tries again instead of giving up.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your block tower falls down. What does a good leader do?

options.label: Try again instead of giving up
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader tries again instead of giving up when a tower falls down.

options.label: Give up and walk away
options.outcome: Giving up means the tower never gets built — trying again is what a good leader does.

options.label: Blame someone else for the fall
options.outcome: Blaming someone else doesn't fix the tower — trying again is a better response.

slides.title: Using Kind Words
slides.text: Kind words help a friend feel better. Saying "let's fix it together" is kind.

widgetConfig.scenario: Something went wrong and a friend feels bad. What kind words help?

options.label: "Let's fix it together"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Kind words like 'let's fix it together' help a friend feel better.

options.label: "This is all your fault"
options.outcome: Blaming a friend doesn't help them feel better — kind words like 'let's fix it together' work much better.

options.label: Say nothing at all
options.outcome: Saying nothing misses a chance to help a friend feel better — kind words make a real difference.

quiz.question: What does a leader do?
choices: Helps a group get things done
Plays alone all the time
quiz.explanation: A leader helps a group work together. Showing friends the rules is one way to help.

quiz.question: You knock over a friend's tower by accident. What should you say?
choices: Sorry
It was not me
quiz.explanation: Saying sorry shows you care about a friend's feelings. It helps them trust you again.

quiz.question: A friend is trying something hard. What can you do?
choices: Cheer them on
Walk away
quiz.explanation: Cheering for a friend helps them feel brave. Clapping when they try something hard is kind.

quiz.question: A leader cleans up first. What happens next?
choices: Friends want to help too
Friends walk away
quiz.explanation: Leading by example means showing how, not just telling. Cleaning up first makes friends want to help too.

quiz.question: You lose a game. What does a good sport say?
choices: Good game
That's not fair
quiz.explanation: A good sport stays kind even after losing. Saying "good game" shows you care about your friend.

quiz.question: A friend dropped their crayons. No one asked you to help. What do you do?
choices: Pick them up
Walk past them
quiz.explanation: Good leaders help even when no one asks. Picking up dropped crayons is a kind, helpful thing to do.

quiz.question: Your plan breaks and things go wrong. What should a good leader do?
choices: Stay calm and think what to do next
Yell and give up
quiz.explanation: Staying calm helps you think of what to do next. Taking a deep breath is a good first step.

quiz.question: You try to build a block tower and it falls down. What should you do?
choices: Try again
Never try again
quiz.explanation: Good leaders keep trying instead of giving up. Building a fallen tower again shows you do not quit.

quiz.question: A friend makes a mistake. What are kind words to say?
choices: That's okay, let's fix it
You did it wrong
quiz.explanation: Kind words help a friend feel better after a mistake. Saying "let's fix it together" shows you care.

quiz.question: Why does a good leader use kind words?
choices: Kind words help friends feel good
Mean words work better
quiz.explanation: Kind words make friends feel good and want to be near you. Saying something nice is an easy way to be kind.

slides.title: Taking Turns
slides.text: Everyone gets a turn to be the leader. Everyone also gets a turn to follow the leader.

widgetConfig.scenario: In your group, does only one person always get to be the leader?

options.label: No — everyone gets a turn to lead and to follow
options.outcome: Exactly right! Everyone gets a turn to be the leader, and everyone also gets a turn to follow the leader.

options.label: Yes, the same person leads forever
options.outcome: The same person leading forever isn't how it works — everyone gets a turn to lead and to follow.

options.label: Only grown-ups can ever be leaders
options.outcome: Kids can be leaders too — everyone gets a turn to lead, not just grown-ups.

slides.title: Working Together
slides.text: A big job is easier with many hands. Friends can each build one part of a tower.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group needs to build a big tower, and everyone wants to do it their own way. What helps the group succeed?

options.label: Working together and combining everyone's ideas
options.outcome: Exactly! Working together as a team usually builds something better than everyone working separately.

options.label: Everyone doing their own separate tower
options.outcome: Separate efforts can end up disorganized — working together usually leads to a better result.

options.label: Only one person doing all the work
options.outcome: Including everyone's help and ideas usually works better than one person doing it all alone.

slides.title: Listening to Friends
slides.text: A good leader listens to what friends say. Listening helps you learn what your friends like.

widgetConfig.scenario: A good leader wants to know what their friends like. What should they do?

options.label: Listen to what friends say
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader listens to what friends say — listening helps you learn what your friends like.

options.label: Only talk about what they like
options.outcome: Only talking about your own likes means you never learn what your friends like — listening helps much more.

options.label: Listening to friends does not matter
options.outcome: Listening to friends actually matters a lot — it helps you learn what they like and care about.

slides.title: Sharing Credit
slides.text: A good leader says, "we did it together." Sharing credit makes the whole team feel proud.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend worked together on a drawing, but someone says "Wow, you drew that all by yourself!" What's the best response?

options.label: "Thanks! My friend helped a lot too."
options.outcome: That's great leadership — giving credit to everyone who helped makes your friend feel valued too.

options.label: Say nothing and just say thank you
options.outcome: It's kind to mention your friend's help — sharing credit makes teamwork feel fair.

options.label: Agree that you did it all alone
options.outcome: That leaves out your friend's hard work — sharing credit is the fair and kind thing to do.

slides.title: Making a Fair Choice
slides.text: A good leader helps the group choose fairly. Taking turns picking is one fair way to choose.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group needs to choose something fairly. What's a fair way?

options.label: Take turns picking
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader helps the group choose fairly, and taking turns picking is one fair way.

options.label: Let the loudest person always decide
options.outcome: Letting the loudest person always decide isn't fair to everyone else — taking turns picking is fairer.

options.label: Fairness does not matter in choices
options.outcome: Fairness actually matters a lot — taking turns picking helps everyone feel included.

slides.title: Welcoming a New Friend
slides.text: A good leader helps new friends feel welcome. Saying "come play with us" makes someone happy.

widgetConfig.scenario: A new kid is standing alone at recess, looking unsure. What's a leader-like thing to do?

options.label: Say "come play with us!"
options.outcome: That's great leadership! Inviting someone in makes them feel welcome and shows kindness.

options.label: Ignore them and keep playing
options.outcome: Ignoring someone who looks left out misses a chance to show leadership and kindness.

options.label: Wait for someone else to invite them
options.outcome: A good leader takes the first step to welcome someone, rather than waiting for someone else to do it.

slides.title: Picking a Team Game
slides.text: Friends may want to play different games. Taking turns picking the game is fair.

widgetConfig.scenario: Friends want to play different games. What's a fair way to pick?

options.label: Take turns picking the game
options.outcome: Exactly right! Friends may want to play different games, and taking turns picking the game is fair.

options.label: Only ever play one person's favorite
options.outcome: Only playing one person's favorite isn't fair to everyone else — taking turns picking is fairer.

options.label: Taking turns picking never works
options.outcome: Taking turns picking actually works well — it gives everyone a fair chance to pick a game they like.

slides.title: Helping a Friend Who Is Stuck
slides.text: A friend may get stuck on a hard puzzle. A good leader stops to help.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend is stuck on a hard puzzle. What does a good leader do?

options.label: Stop and help them
options.outcome: Exactly right! A friend may get stuck on a hard puzzle, and a good leader stops to help.

options.label: Keep playing and ignore them
options.outcome: Ignoring a stuck friend misses a chance to help — stopping to help them is what a good leader does.

options.label: Tell them puzzles are too hard for them
options.outcome: Telling a friend something is too hard for them isn't encouraging — stopping to help is much kinder.

slides.title: Saying Thank You
slides.text: A good leader says thank you for help. It makes friends want to help again.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend helped you with something. What should a good leader say?

options.label: Thank you
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader says thank you for help — it makes friends want to help again.

options.label: Nothing at all
options.outcome: Saying nothing misses a chance to show appreciation — thank you makes friends want to help again.

options.label: Saying thank you does not matter
options.outcome: Saying thank you actually matters a lot — it makes friends want to help again next time.

quiz.question: Should you get a turn to lead?
choices: Yes, everyone gets a turn
No, only one person leads
quiz.explanation: Taking turns to lead is fair for everyone. Today you lead the game, tomorrow a friend leads.

quiz.question: Is a big job easier with many hands?
choices: Yes, it is easier
No, one person should do it alone
quiz.explanation: A big job gets done faster with many hands helping. Building a tower is quicker when everyone builds one part.

quiz.question: A friend tells you their idea. What should a good leader do?
choices: Listen to it
Ignore it
quiz.explanation: A good leader listens when a friend shares an idea. Listening helps you learn what your friends like.

quiz.question: Your team wins. What does a good leader say?
choices: We did it together
I did it all myself
quiz.explanation: Sharing credit makes the whole team feel proud. Saying "we did it together" is kinder than "I did it alone."

quiz.question: Two friends both want to go first. What is a fair way to choose?
choices: Take turns picking
Only the biggest kid decides
quiz.explanation: Taking turns is a fair way to choose who goes first. It means no one always gets picked over the other.

quiz.question: A new kid is standing alone at recess. What should a good leader do?
choices: Say come play with us
Ignore them
quiz.explanation: A good leader helps new friends feel welcome. Saying "come play with us" can make a lonely kid happy.

quiz.question: Your group can't agree which game to play. What can help?
choices: Take turns picking the game
Only one person always picks
quiz.explanation: Taking turns picking the game is fair when friends disagree. Everyone gets a turn to choose what to play.

quiz.question: A friend is stuck and can't finish a puzzle. What can you do?
choices: Help them
Laugh at them
quiz.explanation: A good leader stops to help a friend who is stuck. Helping with a hard puzzle shows you care.

quiz.question: A friend helps you carry your books. What should you say?
choices: Thank you
Nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Saying thank you shows you noticed someone's help. It makes friends want to help you again next time.

quiz.question: Your team builds a great fort together. What should you say?
choices: We built this together
I built this fort
quiz.explanation: Sharing credit makes the whole team feel proud of their work. Saying "we built this together" is kinder than taking all the credit.

slides.title: Listening to Everyone's Ideas
slides.text: A good leader asks what other people think instead of only sharing their own idea. When your group picks a recess game, asking everyone what they want shows real leadership.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group is deciding on a game to play. You have an idea, but so do two others. What should a good leader do?

options.label: Ask what everyone else thinks before deciding
options.outcome: Exactly! Good leaders ask for and value everyone's ideas, not just their own.

options.label: Only share your own idea and ignore the rest
options.outcome: Good leadership means hearing everyone's ideas, not just pushing your own.

options.label: Pick randomly without asking anyone
options.outcome: Asking what others think leads to better decisions than picking randomly without listening.

slides.title: Giving Out Jobs
slides.text: Splitting a group project into smaller jobs and letting each person handle one is called delegation. On a poster project, one person might draw, another might write, and a third might color it in.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group has a poster project. What's a smart way to organize the work?

options.label: Split it into smaller jobs, like draw, write, color
options.outcome: Exactly right! Splitting a group project into smaller jobs and letting each person handle one is called delegation.

options.label: Have one person do everything alone
options.outcome: Having one person do everything alone misses the benefit of splitting up the work — delegation works better.

options.label: Splitting up jobs never helps
options.outcome: Splitting up jobs actually helps a lot — it's called delegation, and it makes group projects more manageable.

slides.title: Setting a Group Goal
slides.text: Deciding together what the group is trying to achieve makes it easier to know if things are working. Agreeing the goal is "finish the poster by Friday" gives everyone something clear to aim for.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group is building a fort but everyone has different ideas with no clear plan. What should a leader do?

options.label: Help the group agree on one clear goal to work toward
options.outcome: Great leadership move! A clear shared goal helps everyone work together instead of pulling in different directions.

options.label: Let everyone keep doing their own separate thing
options.outcome: Without a shared goal, the group's efforts can end up scattered and the fort might not come together well.

options.label: Just pick the goal yourself without asking anyone
options.outcome: Including the group in setting the goal (even if you guide it) usually works better than deciding alone.

slides.title: Leading by Example
slides.text: Doing the right thing yourself, like helping clean up, often gets others to join in too. Starting to tidy the classroom without being asked usually works better than just telling classmates to do it.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want classmates to help clean up. What works better than just telling them to?

options.label: Start tidying up yourself without being asked
options.outcome: Exactly right! Doing the right thing yourself, like starting to tidy up, often gets others to join in too.

options.label: Just order everyone else to do it
options.outcome: Just ordering others to do it usually works less well than starting the work yourself first.

options.label: Leading by example never works
options.outcome: Leading by example actually works really well — starting the work yourself often gets others to join in.

slides.title: Taking Responsibility
slides.text: If you agree to do a job, finishing it even when it is not fun builds real trust. Bringing the markers you promised, even on a day you'd rather relax, shows you can be counted on.

widgetConfig.scenario: You promised to bring markers for group art, but you'd rather relax today. What builds trust?

options.label: Bring the markers like you promised
options.outcome: Exactly right! Finishing a job you agreed to, even when it's not fun, builds real trust with your team.

options.label: Skip it since you do not feel like it
options.outcome: Skipping it after promising can break trust — following through even when it's inconvenient builds real trust.

options.label: Promises do not need to be kept
options.outcome: Promises actually need to be kept — following through, even when it's not fun, is what builds real trust.

slides.title: Motivating Others
slides.text: A good leader notices small wins and points them out to keep the team's energy up. Saying "we already finished two parts, we've got this" can help tired teammates keep going.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your teammate is discouraged because their part of the group project isn't going well. What's the best way to help as a leader?

options.label: Point out what they've done well and offer to help with what's left
options.outcome: That's great leadership — specific encouragement plus real help motivates people far more than just saying "try harder."

options.label: Tell them to just work faster
options.outcome: Just telling someone to work faster doesn't address why they're discouraged — specific encouragement and help works better.

options.label: Redo their part yourself without asking
options.outcome: Taking over can make them feel like they failed. Helping them finish their own part builds their confidence instead.

slides.title: Planning the Steps
slides.text: A good leader thinks through the steps of a project before starting, so the group doesn't run out of time. Listing what needs to happen each day before a science fair, instead of starting the night before, helps the whole team stay on track.

widgetConfig.scenario: A science fair is coming up. What helps the team avoid running out of time?

options.label: List what needs to happen each day ahead of time
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader thinks through the steps before starting, so the group doesn't run out of time.

options.label: Start the night before
options.outcome: Starting the night before often leads to running out of time — planning ahead works much better.

options.label: Planning ahead never helps a project
options.outcome: Planning ahead actually helps a lot — it keeps the whole team on track instead of scrambling at the last minute.

slides.title: Staying Positive When It's Hard
slides.text: When a project gets frustrating, a good leader keeps a hopeful attitude instead of complaining, which helps the whole team keep going. Saying "we've solved harder problems than this" during a tricky group assignment can lift everyone's mood.

widgetConfig.scenario: A group project gets frustrating. What helps the team keep going?

options.label: Keep a hopeful attitude instead of complaining
options.outcome: Exactly right! When a project gets frustrating, a good leader keeps a hopeful attitude, which helps the whole team keep going.

options.label: Complain loudly about how hard it is
options.outcome: Complaining loudly can bring the whole team's mood down — staying hopeful helps everyone keep going instead.

options.label: A leader's attitude never affects the team
options.outcome: A leader's attitude actually affects the team a lot — staying positive can lift everyone's mood during a hard project.

slides.title: Checking In On the Team
slides.text: A good leader checks partway through a project to see how everyone is doing, instead of waiting until the deadline to find out something went wrong. Asking "how's your part coming along?" halfway through a group project can catch problems while there's still time to fix them.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're halfway through a group project. What's a smart leader move?

options.label: Ask "how's your part coming along?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader checks partway through a project, which can catch problems while there's still time to fix them.

options.label: Wait until the deadline to check anything
options.outcome: Waiting until the deadline means problems get caught too late — checking in partway through is much smarter.

options.label: Checking in partway through never helps
options.outcome: Checking in partway through actually helps a lot — it catches problems while there's still time to fix them.

quiz.question: Deciding what to play at recess, what does a good leader do with other people's ideas?
choices: Listens to them
Ignores them and shares only their own
quiz.explanation: A good leader asks what other people think instead of only sharing their own idea. If everyone wants a different game, listening helps the group find something fair to play.

quiz.question: On a group poster, one person draws, one writes, one colors. What is this splitting of jobs called?
choices: Delegation
Doing every part of a job yourself
quiz.explanation: Delegation means splitting a job into smaller parts so each person does one piece. On a poster, one person might draw while another writes, so the work gets done faster.

quiz.question: You agreed to bring markers for a project. Why does following through matter?
choices: It builds trust
It doesn't matter at all
quiz.explanation: Following through on a promise, even when it's not fun, shows people they can count on you. Bringing markers you promised to bring, instead of forgetting, is how trust gets built.

quiz.question: You start cleaning the classroom without being asked, and others join in. What is this?
choices: Leading by example
Only telling others what to do
quiz.explanation: Leading by example means doing the right thing yourself instead of just telling others to do it. When you start cleaning without being asked, classmates often join in too.

quiz.question: Which is a clearer goal for a group project: "finish the poster by Friday" or "let's just do our best"?
choices: "Finish the poster by Friday" — clear and specific
"Let's just do our best" — vague
quiz.explanation: A clear goal, like "finish the poster by Friday," tells everyone exactly what to aim for. A vague goal like "do our best" doesn't say when or how you'll know you succeeded.

quiz.question: Your team already finished two parts of a project. What can a good leader say to keep spirits up?
choices: We've already finished two parts, we've got this
Stop wasting time and hurry up
quiz.explanation: Pointing out small wins, like finishing two parts already, helps a tired team keep going. It reminds everyone how much progress they've already made.

quiz.question: Before starting a science fair project, what should a good leader do?
choices: List the steps and plan the timing
Just start and figure it out later
quiz.explanation: Planning the steps before starting helps a group avoid running out of time. Listing what needs to happen each day, instead of starting the night before, keeps everyone on track.

quiz.question: A group project gets frustrating. What helps the team keep going?
choices: A leader staying positive and hopeful
A leader complaining along with everyone
quiz.explanation: A leader's hopeful attitude can lift the whole team's mood when a project gets hard. Saying "we've solved harder problems than this" helps everyone keep trying instead of giving up.

quiz.question: Halfway through a group project, what should a good leader do?
choices: Check in on how everyone's part is going
Wait until the deadline to check anything
quiz.explanation: Checking in partway through a project, by asking how everyone's part is going, can catch problems early. Waiting until the deadline to find out something went wrong is often too late to fix it.

quiz.question: One teammate loves drawing, another loves writing. What should a good leader do when giving out jobs?
choices: Match each job to what they're good at
Assign jobs randomly without thinking
quiz.explanation: Delegation works best when jobs match each person's strengths, like giving the drawing to someone who loves art. This helps the whole project turn out better than assigning jobs randomly.

slides.title: Solving a Disagreement
slides.text: When two people in a group disagree, a good leader lets both sides explain their thinking. Suggesting a compromise, like using both colors two teammates wanted, often helps everyone feel heard.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two teammates disagree about which color to use. What helps?

options.label: Suggest a compromise, like using both colors
options.outcome: Exactly right! Suggesting a compromise, like using both colors two teammates wanted, often helps everyone feel heard.

options.label: Pick a side and ignore the other person
options.outcome: Picking a side and ignoring the other person can leave them feeling unheard — a compromise works much better.

options.label: Disagreements should never be addressed
options.outcome: Disagreements actually need to be addressed — a good leader lets both sides explain and finds a compromise.

slides.title: Speaking Up for Someone
slides.text: When someone in the group is being left out, a good leader helps them get a chance to speak. Saying "let's hear what they think too" is a small but real act of leadership.

widgetConfig.scenario: You notice someone being teased during group work. What's a good leadership move?

options.label: Speak up and say the teasing should stop
options.outcome: Great leadership! Speaking up for someone being treated unfairly shows real courage and care.

options.label: Stay quiet so you don't get involved
options.outcome: Staying silent can let unfair treatment continue — speaking up, even briefly, can make a real difference.

options.label: Join in with the teasing
options.outcome: Joining in makes things worse — speaking up against it is the stronger leadership choice.

slides.title: Encouraging a Teammate
slides.text: Noticing when someone on your team is struggling and offering to help is real leadership. Asking "do you want help with that part?" shows you care about the whole team's success.

widgetConfig.scenario: You notice a teammate struggling with their part of a group project. What's a good leader move?

options.label: Offer to help them
options.outcome: Exactly! Noticing when someone on your team is struggling and offering to help shows real leadership.

options.label: Ignore them since it's not your job
options.outcome: Ignoring a struggling teammate misses a chance to support the team — a good leader offers to help.

options.label: Point out that they are struggling in front of everyone
options.outcome: Calling it out publicly can embarrass them — quietly offering to help is the better leadership move.

slides.title: Giving Credit to Others
slides.text: A good leader points out what teammates did well instead of keeping the praise for themselves. Saying "Maya's idea made this project great" makes the whole team want to keep contributing.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate's idea made the project great. What should a good leader say?

options.label: "Maya's idea made this project great"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader points out what teammates did well, which makes the whole team want to keep contributing.

options.label: Take all the credit for yourself
options.outcome: Taking all the credit yourself can discourage teammates from contributing — giving credit to others works much better.

options.label: Giving credit to others never matters
options.outcome: Giving credit to others actually matters a lot — it makes the whole team want to keep contributing.

slides.title: Making a Group Decision Fairly
slides.text: When a group cannot agree, a good leader might suggest a vote so everyone gets a say. A fair decision usually feels better to the team, even to people whose idea was not picked.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group can't agree on a decision. What's a fair way to decide?

options.label: Suggest a vote so everyone gets a say
options.outcome: Exactly right! When a group cannot agree, a good leader might suggest a vote so everyone gets a say.

options.label: Let the leader decide alone every time
options.outcome: Letting the leader decide alone every time can leave others feeling unheard — a vote gives everyone a say.

options.label: Fair decisions never matter to a team
options.outcome: Fair decisions actually matter a lot — they tend to feel better to the team, even for those whose idea wasn't picked.

slides.title: Admitting a Mistake as a Leader
slides.text: A good leader owns up when their own choice caused a problem for the group. Saying "I picked the wrong plan, let's fix it together" earns more respect than hiding the mistake.

widgetConfig.scenario: As the team captain, you picked the wrong strategy and your team lost the game. What's the best thing to say to your team?

options.label: "That strategy was my call and it didn't work — let's figure out a better one together."
options.outcome: That's real leadership — owning your mistake openly builds trust and shows the team it's okay to take risks and learn.

options.label: Blame a teammate for not following the plan well enough
options.outcome: Blaming others for your own decision damages trust — owning the mistake yourself is stronger leadership.

options.label: Pretend it wasn't a big deal and move on without discussing it
options.outcome: Not addressing it means missing a chance to learn and show accountability — owning it builds more respect.

slides.title: Handling Being Disagreed With
slides.text: Sometimes teammates push back on a leader's own idea, and a good leader listens instead of getting defensive. If a teammate says your plan for the presentation won't work, asking "what would you do differently?" is more useful than insisting you're right.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate says your plan won't work. What's the better response?

options.label: Ask "what would you do differently?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader listens instead of getting defensive when a teammate pushes back on their idea.

options.label: Insist you are right and ignore them
options.outcome: Insisting you're right and ignoring them can shut down useful feedback — asking what they'd do differently is more useful.

options.label: Listening to pushback never helps
options.outcome: Listening to pushback actually helps a lot — it can reveal a better way to do something.

slides.title: Staying Fair, Even With Friends
slides.text: A good leader gives the best job to whoever is best suited for it, not just to their closest friend. Picking the strongest reader for the tricky research part, even if a friend wanted it, keeps the whole project fair and strong.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your friend wants the tricky research part, but another teammate is better suited for it. What's fair?

options.label: Give the job to whoever is best suited for it
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader gives the best job to whoever is best suited for it, not just to their closest friend.

options.label: Always give the best job to your closest friend
options.outcome: Always favoring your closest friend isn't fair to the rest of the team — picking who's best suited keeps things fair.

options.label: Fairness does not matter when friends are involved
options.outcome: Fairness actually matters even more when friends are involved — it keeps the whole project fair and strong.

slides.title: Calming Down an Upset Teammate
slides.text: When a teammate gets frustrated or upset, a good leader helps them calm down before trying to solve the problem. Saying "let's take a breath and figure this out together" helps an upset teammate feel heard instead of more annoyed.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate is frustrated and upset. What should a good leader do first?

options.label: Help them calm down before solving the problem
options.outcome: Exactly right! When a teammate gets frustrated, a good leader helps them calm down before trying to solve the problem.

options.label: Ignore their feelings and push forward
options.outcome: Ignoring their feelings and pushing forward can make them feel more annoyed — calming them down first works much better.

options.label: Calming someone down never helps solve a problem
options.outcome: Calming someone down actually helps a lot — it makes them feel heard before tackling the problem together.

quiz.question: Two teammates disagree about a paint color. What helps solve it?
choices: Letting both sides say what they think
Only listening to one side
quiz.explanation: Hearing both sides of a disagreement helps you find an answer everyone can accept. If two friends want different colors, using both is often better than picking just one.

quiz.question: A quiet group member hasn't shared their idea yet. What should you do?
choices: Help make sure they get to speak
Ignore it and move on
quiz.explanation: A good leader notices when someone hasn't had a chance to speak and helps include them. Asking a quiet teammate what they think shows everyone's ideas matter.

quiz.question: A teammate's idea made the project great. What should a good leader say?
choices: Point out that it was their idea
Let people think it was the leader's idea
quiz.explanation: Giving credit to whoever had the idea makes the whole team want to keep contributing. Saying "that was Maya's idea" feels better to everyone than letting people think it was yours.

quiz.question: A group can't agree on a plan. What can help everyone feel it was fair?
choices: Taking a vote so everyone gets a say
The leader just picking their favorite
quiz.explanation: Taking a vote gives everyone a say, which helps a decision feel fair. Even someone whose idea loses the vote usually feels better than if the leader just picked alone.

quiz.question: A leader's own plan caused a problem for the group. What should they do?
choices: Own up to the mistake and help fix it
Hide it and hope no one notices
quiz.explanation: Owning up to a mistake and helping fix it earns more respect than hiding it. Saying "I picked the wrong plan, let's fix it together" shows real leadership.

quiz.question: A teammate is struggling with their part of the project. What can a good leader do?
choices: Offer to help them
Ignore it and hope it works out
quiz.explanation: Noticing a struggling teammate and offering to help is real leadership, not just doing your own part well. Asking "do you want help with that?" shows you care about the team's success.

quiz.question: A teammate says your presentation plan won't work. What should a good leader do?
choices: Listen and ask what they'd do differently
Get defensive and insist you're right
quiz.explanation: Listening to pushback instead of getting defensive usually leads to a better plan. Asking "what would you do differently?" often uncovers a problem you hadn't noticed.

quiz.question: Your friend wants the hardest research job, but another teammate is a stronger reader. What should a fair leader do?
choices: Give the job to whoever fits it best
Give it to your friend no matter what
quiz.explanation: Staying fair means giving a job to whoever fits it best, even if that's not your friend. This keeps the whole project stronger and shows you're not just playing favorites.

quiz.question: A teammate gets upset and frustrated. What should a good leader do first?
choices: Help them calm down before problem-solving
Ignore their feelings and move on
quiz.explanation: Helping someone calm down before solving the problem makes them feel heard, not rushed. Saying "let's take a breath and figure this out together" often works better than jumping straight to solutions.

quiz.question: Two teammates want the last spot on the presentation team. What's the fairest way to decide?
choices: Let the group vote or find another fair way
Just pick your favorite teammate
quiz.explanation: Letting the group vote, instead of just picking a favorite, helps a decision feel fair to everyone. A fair process matters just as much as the final choice.

slides.title: Being accountable
slides.text: When something goes wrong on a team, a good leader looks at what they could have done differently, not just who else to blame. For example, if your group misses a deadline, a good leader asks "what could I have communicated better?" instead of immediately pointing fingers at whoever finished last.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group misses a deadline. What does a good leader ask first?

options.label: "What could I have communicated better?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! When something goes wrong, a good leader looks at what they could have done differently, not just who else to blame.

options.label: Immediately blame whoever finished last
options.outcome: Immediately blaming whoever finished last skips a chance to reflect on what the leader could have done better.

options.label: Accountability never matters to a leader
options.outcome: Accountability actually matters a lot — reflecting on your own part builds trust and improves the next project.

slides.title: Earning trust over time
slides.text: Trust is built slowly, through many small kept promises, and can be lost quickly by breaking just one. For example, consistently showing up on time and finishing your part of group work, week after week, slowly builds real trust — but missing one important deadline right before a big presentation can undo a lot of that trust quickly.

widgetConfig.scenario: How is trust within a team usually built?

options.label: Slowly, through many small kept promises
options.outcome: Exactly right! Trust is built slowly, through many small kept promises, and can be lost quickly if those promises break.

options.label: Instantly, the moment someone becomes the leader
options.outcome: Trust isn't automatic just from a title — it's built slowly through consistently kept promises.

options.label: Trust can't actually be built or lost
options.outcome: Trust absolutely can be built or lost — it grows through kept promises and can be damaged by broken ones.

slides.title: Leading by example
slides.text: A leader who does the hard, unglamorous work themselves earns more buy-in than one who only assigns it to others. For example, a team captain who shows up early to set up equipment, instead of just telling teammates to do it, makes everyone more willing to pitch in without being asked.

widgetConfig.scenario: A team captain shows up early to set up equipment instead of just telling others to. What does this do?

options.label: Earns more buy-in than just assigning the task
options.outcome: Exactly right! A leader who does the hard, unglamorous work themselves earns more buy-in than one who only assigns it to others.

options.label: Makes no difference to the team
options.outcome: It actually makes a real difference — doing the hard work yourself earns more buy-in from the team.

options.label: Doing the work yourself is a waste of a leader's time
options.outcome: Doing the work yourself isn't a waste — it earns more buy-in and makes teammates more willing to pitch in.

slides.title: Staying humble
slides.text: Being willing to admit you don't have all the answers, and asking for help, actually builds more respect than pretending to know everything. For example, if you're leading a project and genuinely don't know how to solve a technical problem, admitting "I'm not sure, does anyone have an idea?" earns more respect than bluffing your way through and getting it wrong.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're leading a project and don't know how to solve a technical problem. What builds more respect?

options.label: Admitting it and asking if anyone has an idea
options.outcome: Exactly right! Being willing to admit you don't have all the answers actually builds more respect than pretending to know everything.

options.label: Bluffing your way through and getting it wrong
options.outcome: Bluffing and getting it wrong tends to damage respect more than simply admitting you're unsure.

options.label: Pretending to know everything always
options.outcome: Pretending to know everything doesn't build respect — admitting uncertainty and asking for help actually earns more.

slides.title: Consistency under pressure
slides.text: A leader who behaves the same way whether things are going well or badly earns more trust than one who is only pleasant when things are easy. For example, a team captain who stays even-tempered after a disappointing practice, not just after a win, shows teammates they can count on them no matter what's happening.

widgetConfig.scenario: A team captain stays even-tempered after both a win and a loss. What does this build?

options.label: More trust, since teammates can count on them
options.outcome: Exactly right! A leader who behaves the same way whether things are going well or badly earns more trust than one who's only pleasant when easy.

options.label: Nothing — moods never affect trust
options.outcome: Moods actually affect trust quite a bit — staying consistent, even after a loss, shows teammates they can count on you.

options.label: Trust only comes from celebrating wins
options.outcome: Trust doesn't only come from wins — staying even-tempered after a loss too is what really builds lasting trust.

slides.title: Following through on small promises
slides.text: Trust often depends more on small, repeated promises than on one big grand gesture. For example, consistently sending the meeting notes you promised, week after week, does more for a leader's reputation than one impressive speech.

widgetConfig.scenario: You told a teammate you'd bring extra supplies tomorrow, but you forgot. What's the best next step?

options.label: Apologize, bring them as soon as you can, and be more careful next time
options.outcome: Right approach — small broken promises add up to lost trust over time, but owning it quickly and following through shows you take your word seriously.

options.label: Don't mention it and hope they forgot too
options.outcome: Ignoring it can quietly erode trust — even small promises matter to how much people can rely on you.

options.label: Make an excuse so it doesn't seem like your fault
options.outcome: Making excuses instead of owning it can damage trust more than the mistake itself — a simple apology and follow-through works better.

slides.title: Standing up for what's right
slides.text: A leader who does the right thing even when it's unpopular or less convenient earns respect over time. For example, if a teammate suggests copying another group's idea, a leader who says "let's come up with our own," even though it's more work, models real integrity for the team.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate suggests copying another group's idea. What does a leader with integrity say?

options.label: "Let's come up with our own"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A leader who does the right thing even when it's less convenient, like insisting on original work, earns respect over time.

options.label: Agree to copy it since it is easier
options.outcome: Agreeing to copy it, even though it's easier, doesn't model the integrity that earns respect over time.

options.label: Standing up for what is right never matters
options.outcome: Standing up for what's right actually matters a lot — it models real integrity for the whole team.

slides.title: Recovering trust after a mistake
slides.text: Trust that's broken by one missed deadline can be slowly rebuilt through consistent follow-through afterward. For example, a leader who missed a deadline can rebuild trust by hitting every deadline afterward and communicating early if something might slip again.

widgetConfig.scenario: You missed a deadline once. How can you rebuild trust afterward?

options.label: Hit every deadline afterward and communicate early if something might slip
options.outcome: Exactly right! Trust broken by one missed deadline can be slowly rebuilt through consistent follow-through afterward.

options.label: Trust can never be rebuilt after one mistake
options.outcome: Trust actually can be rebuilt — consistent follow-through after a mistake slowly restores it.

options.label: Ignore it and hope nobody remembers
options.outcome: Ignoring it and hoping nobody remembers doesn't rebuild trust — consistent follow-through afterward does.

slides.title: Doing the right thing when no one's watching
slides.text: A leader's character often shows most clearly in the choices nobody else would ever find out about. For example, giving credit for an idea to the teammate who actually thought of it, even when no one would have noticed if you'd kept it for yourself, is exactly the kind of quiet integrity that earns lasting trust.

widgetConfig.scenario: No one would notice if you skipped a step in a task meant to keep things fair for your team. What should you do?

options.label: Do it right anyway, since integrity matters even unseen
options.outcome: Exactly — real character shows in what you do when no one's watching. That consistency is what makes people trust you as a leader.

options.label: Skip it since no one would know
options.outcome: Cutting corners when no one's watching can become a habit, and it undermines the trust that real leadership depends on.

options.label: Only do things right when being observed
options.outcome: Leaders who are only honest when watched don't build the same deep trust as those who do right consistently.

quiz.question: Your group misses a deadline. What does "being accountable" look like?
choices: Looking at your own part in what went wrong
Immediately blaming someone else
quiz.explanation: Accountability means looking at your own role in a problem instead of only blaming others. For example, if your group misses a deadline, asking "what could I have communicated better?" is more useful than pointing fingers, because it actually helps fix things next time.

quiz.question: How is trust usually built, based on showing up consistently over weeks?
choices: Slowly, through many small kept promises
Instantly, the moment someone becomes a leader
quiz.explanation: Trust builds gradually through many small kept promises, like showing up on time week after week. But it can be lost quickly, since missing one important deadline right before a big presentation can undo weeks of that trust almost instantly.

quiz.question: A team captain shows up early to set up equipment instead of just assigning it. What does this show?
choices: Leading by example earns more buy-in
Leaders should never do hands-on work
quiz.explanation: Doing the hard, unglamorous work yourself, like setting up equipment early, earns more willingness from teammates than just assigning it to them. When people see a leader pitching in, they're more likely to pitch in too, without needing to be asked.

quiz.question: Leading a project, you genuinely don't know how to fix a technical problem. What earns more respect?
choices: Admitting it and asking for help
Bluffing your way through it
quiz.explanation: Staying humble means admitting when you don't have all the answers instead of pretending to. Saying "I'm not sure, does anyone have an idea?" during a tricky problem actually earns more respect than bluffing and getting it wrong.

quiz.question: A team captain stays even-tempered after a tough loss, not just after wins. What does this build?
choices: Trust, through consistency in good times and bad
Trust only matters after a win
quiz.explanation: A leader who acts the same way after a loss as after a win shows teammates they can be counted on no matter what. That kind of consistency, staying even-tempered through both good and bad moments, builds far more trust than only being pleasant when things go well.

quiz.question: Which builds a leader's reputation more over time?
choices: Consistently keeping small promises, like sending notes every week
One impressive speech
quiz.explanation: Trust usually comes from many small, repeated promises rather than one big impressive moment. A leader who consistently sends the notes they promised, week after week, builds a stronger reputation than someone who gives one great speech and then disappears.

quiz.question: A teammate wants to copy another group's idea. What should a leader with integrity do?
choices: Say let's come up with our own, even if it's more work
Go along with copying since it's easier
quiz.explanation: Standing up for what's right, even when it's less convenient, is what earns lasting respect. Saying "let's come up with our own idea" instead of copying another group's work is more effort, but it shows real integrity.

quiz.question: A leader missed an important deadline. How can they rebuild the team's trust afterward?
choices: Hit every deadline afterward and communicate early
Avoid the topic and hope it's forgotten
quiz.explanation: Trust that's damaged by one mistake, like a missed deadline, can be rebuilt through consistent follow-through afterward. Hitting every deadline from then on, and communicating early if something might slip, slowly shows the team they can rely on you again.

quiz.question: You could take credit for a teammate's idea and no one would ever know. What should you do?
choices: Give credit to the teammate anyway
Take the credit since no one would find out
quiz.explanation: Doing the right thing even when nobody would ever find out is a real test of character. Giving credit to the teammate who actually had the idea, instead of quietly keeping it for yourself, is exactly the kind of quiet integrity that earns lasting trust.

quiz.question: A leader's team suggests a totally different plan than the leader's, and it seems solid. What should a humble leader do?
choices: Consider adopting the team's plan
Insist on their own plan since they're the leader
quiz.explanation: Staying humble means being genuinely open to a better idea, even when it isn't your own. A leader who considers adopting the team's plan instead of insisting on their own, just because they're in charge, usually ends up with a stronger outcome.

slides.title: Matching jobs to strengths
slides.text: A good leader notices what each person is good at and hands out jobs that fit, instead of assigning randomly. For example, on a group science project, giving the research job to someone who loves reading, the presentation to someone who enjoys public speaking, and the data charts to someone good at math sets everyone up to actually succeed.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're assigning tasks for a group project. One teammate loves writing, another loves art. What's the smart approach?

options.label: Match each person's task to their strengths
options.outcome: Great leadership! Matching tasks to people's strengths usually leads to better results and happier teammates.

options.label: Assign tasks completely randomly
options.outcome: Random assignment can waste people's natural talents — matching tasks to strengths usually works better.

options.label: Make everyone do the same thing
options.outcome: Letting people use their individual strengths usually produces better results than making everyone do identical tasks.

slides.title: Giving feedback kindly
slides.text: Telling a teammate what could improve, specifically and kindly, helps them grow instead of just feeling criticized. For example, saying "your section is great, maybe just add one more example to make it clearer" helps a teammate improve, while just saying "this part is weak" leaves them with nothing useful to act on.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate's work could improve. What's the best way to tell them?

options.label: Specifically and kindly explain what could improve
options.outcome: Exactly! Telling a teammate what could improve, specifically and kindly, helps them grow without discouraging them.

options.label: Say nothing and let them keep making the same mistake
options.outcome: Staying silent doesn't help them improve — kind, specific feedback does.

options.label: Criticize them harshly in front of the whole team
options.outcome: Harsh public criticism can discourage someone rather than help — specific, kind feedback works much better.

slides.title: Listening actively
slides.text: Really listening means asking follow-up questions and repeating back what you heard, not just waiting for your turn to talk. For example, asking a teammate "so you're worried we won't finish in time, is that right?" shows you were actually listening, not just planning what to say next.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate says they're worried about finishing in time. What shows you're really listening?

options.label: Repeat back "so you're worried we won't finish, is that right?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Really listening means asking follow-up questions and repeating back what you heard, not just waiting for your turn to talk.

options.label: Just plan what you will say next
options.outcome: Just planning what to say next means you're not really listening — repeating back what you heard shows you actually are.

options.label: Listening actively never matters to a team
options.outcome: Listening actively actually matters a lot — it shows teammates you're truly paying attention to their concerns.

slides.title: Motivating a team
slides.text: A good leader notices what actually matters to each teammate and connects the work to it, instead of using the same pep talk for everyone. For example, reminding a teammate who loves art that their design skills are the reason the project looks great can motivate them more than a generic "good job, keep going."

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate loves art and did the design work. What's more motivating than a generic 'good job'?

options.label: Reminding them their design skills made the project great
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader notices what actually matters to each teammate and connects the work to it, instead of a generic pep talk.

options.label: The exact same pep talk for everyone
options.outcome: The same generic pep talk for everyone tends to be less motivating than connecting to what actually matters to each person.

options.label: Motivation never depends on what matters to someone
options.outcome: Motivation actually depends a lot on what matters to each person — connecting to that is far more effective than a generic comment.

slides.title: Recognizing different working styles
slides.text: Some teammates work best with a clear plan laid out step by step, while others do better brainstorming freely before settling on an approach, and a good leader adapts rather than forcing one style on everyone. For example, giving a detail-oriented teammate a checklist while letting a creative teammate free-write ideas first can get better results from both.

widgetConfig.scenario: One teammate likes step-by-step plans, another likes brainstorming freely. What should a good leader do?

options.label: Adapt to each person's working style
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader adapts rather than forcing one working style on everyone, getting better results from both people.

options.label: Force everyone into the same style
options.outcome: Forcing everyone into the same style can get worse results — adapting to each person's style works much better.

options.label: Working styles never actually differ between people
options.outcome: Working styles actually differ quite a bit between people — adapting to them gets better results from everyone.

slides.title: Asking instead of telling
slides.text: A leader who asks a teammate how they'd like to approach a task, instead of just assigning exact steps, usually gets more thoughtful, engaged work in return. For example, asking "how do you want to tackle the research section?" often produces a better outcome than dictating every step.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want a teammate to research a topic. What gets more thoughtful, engaged work?

options.label: Ask "how do you want to tackle this?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A leader who asks a teammate how they'd like to approach a task usually gets more thoughtful, engaged work in return.

options.label: Dictate every single step
options.outcome: Dictating every step tends to produce less engaged work than asking how someone wants to approach it.

options.label: Asking for input never improves the outcome
options.outcome: Asking for input actually improves the outcome a lot — it often leads to more thoughtful, engaged work.

slides.title: Handling an unmotivated teammate
slides.text: A good leader tries to find out why a teammate seems checked out before assuming they're just being lazy. For example, a teammate who suddenly stops contributing might be overwhelmed by something else going on, and a quick, private check-in can uncover that reason.

widgetConfig.scenario: One of your group members isn't contributing to a project, and the deadline is close. What's the best leadership move?

options.label: Talk to them privately to understand what's going on
options.outcome: Good instinct — there's often a reason behind low motivation (confusion, overwhelm, etc.), and a private conversation uncovers it without embarrassing them.

options.label: Call them out in front of the whole group
options.outcome: Calling someone out publicly usually makes them defensive rather than motivated — a private conversation works better.

options.label: Quietly do their part yourself so the project gets done
options.outcome: Doing their work for them solves the project but not the real issue, and it can feel unfair to the rest of the team.

slides.title: Balancing group work fairly
slides.text: Noticing when one teammate is doing far more than their fair share and redistributing tasks keeps a team functioning well and prevents resentment. For example, if one person has ended up with three tasks and another has none, a good leader rebalances the work before it becomes a problem.

widgetConfig.scenario: One teammate has three tasks, another has none. What should a good leader do?

options.label: Rebalance the tasks before it becomes a problem
options.outcome: Exactly right! Noticing uneven work and redistributing tasks keeps a team functioning well and prevents resentment.

options.label: Let it be, since it is not a big deal
options.outcome: Letting uneven work slide can build resentment over time — rebalancing it early prevents that problem.

options.label: Uneven work never causes resentment
options.outcome: Uneven work can actually cause real resentment — rebalancing tasks early keeps the team functioning well.

slides.title: Running an effective meeting
slides.text: Keeping a short group check-in focused on what's actually needed helps a team get things done instead of wasting everyone's time. For example, starting a group meeting with "let's each share what we finished and what we're stuck on" keeps the conversation efficient and useful.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're starting a group check-in. What keeps it efficient?

options.label: Ask everyone to share what's done and what they're stuck on
options.outcome: Exactly right! Keeping a short group check-in focused on what's actually needed helps a team get things done instead of wasting time.

options.label: Let the meeting wander with no focus
options.outcome: Letting a meeting wander wastes everyone's time — a focused check-in gets things done much faster.

options.label: Focused meetings never save time
options.outcome: Focused meetings actually save a lot of time — they keep the conversation efficient and useful.

quiz.question: On a science project, why give research to a reader and presenting to a good public speaker?
choices: It sets each person up to succeed
Strengths don't matter for team jobs
quiz.explanation: Matching tasks to what each person is good at, like giving research to someone who loves reading, sets everyone up to succeed. Random assignments waste people's strengths and often produce weaker results.

quiz.question: Which is more helpful: "this part is weak" or "great section, maybe add one more example"?
choices: "great section, maybe add one more example" — specific and kind
Being vague and harsh
quiz.explanation: Specific, kind feedback, like "add one more example," tells a teammate exactly what to improve. A vague comment like "this part is weak" leaves them with nothing useful to actually act on.

quiz.question: Asking a teammate "so you're worried we won't finish, is that right?" is an example of what?
choices: Listening actively
Waiting for your turn to talk
quiz.explanation: Active listening means checking that you understood, not just waiting for your turn to talk. Asking "so you're worried we won't finish in time, is that right?" shows a teammate you were really paying attention.

quiz.question: A teammate loves art, and you remind them their design skills made the project look great. What is this an example of?
choices: Motivating by connecting to what matters to them
Using the same pep talk for everyone
quiz.explanation: Connecting work to what a teammate personally cares about, like reminding an artist that their design made the project shine, motivates better than a generic "good job." People try harder when they feel their specific contribution matters.

quiz.question: One teammate wants a clear checklist, another prefers to brainstorm freely. What should a good leader do?
choices: Adapt to each person's working style
Force everyone to work the same way
quiz.explanation: Some people work best with a step-by-step checklist, while others do better brainstorming freely first. A good leader adapts to each teammate's style instead of forcing everyone to work the same way, which gets better results from both.

quiz.question: Instead of assigning exact steps for the research section, what could a leader ask?
choices: How do you want to tackle this part?
Just do it exactly this way
quiz.explanation: Asking a teammate how they'd like to tackle a task, instead of dictating every step, usually leads to more thoughtful, engaged work. People tend to care more about a plan they helped create.

quiz.question: A teammate suddenly stops contributing to the group project. What should a good leader do first?
choices: Check in privately to find out why
Assume they're lazy and give up on them
quiz.explanation: A teammate who suddenly stops contributing might be overwhelmed by something else, not just lazy. Checking in privately, instead of assuming the worst, often uncovers the real reason and how to help.

quiz.question: One teammate has three tasks and another has none. What should a fair leader do?
choices: Rebalance the tasks
Leave it as is
quiz.explanation: Noticing when one teammate has three tasks and another has none, and rebalancing the work, keeps a team functioning well. Left alone, an unfair workload usually leads to resentment and burnout.

quiz.question: What's a good way to start a group check-in meeting?
choices: Have everyone share what's done and what they're stuck on
Let the meeting wander with no structure
quiz.explanation: Starting a meeting with a clear focus, like asking everyone what they finished and what they're stuck on, keeps a group from wasting time. A focused check-in gets real information instead of just chatting.

quiz.question: A quiet teammate rarely speaks up in big meetings, but has good ideas one-on-one. What could a good leader do?
choices: Create chances for them to share ideas privately or in smaller groups
Only rely on people who speak up in big meetings
quiz.explanation: A quiet teammate might have great ideas but feel uncomfortable sharing them in a big group. Creating chances to talk privately or in smaller groups helps a good leader hear ideas that would otherwise go unheard.

slides.title: Setting a clear vision
slides.text: A leader who can explain exactly what success looks like gives the team something real to aim for, instead of vague effort. For example, saying "we want every judge to remember our project by name" gives a team a clearer target than just saying "let's do our best."

widgetConfig.scenario: Your team is starting a big project but isn't sure what success looks like. What's the leader's first job?

options.label: Help the team define a clear, shared vision of success
options.outcome: Exactly — a clear vision gives the whole team a shared target to aim for, which makes everything else easier to plan.

options.label: Just start working without a plan
options.outcome: Starting without a clear vision often leads to wasted effort — defining success first helps guide everyone's work.

options.label: Wait for someone else to figure it out
options.outcome: As the leader, helping set that vision is an important part of the role, not something to leave to chance.

slides.title: Fair conflict resolution
slides.text: Listening to both sides of a disagreement fully, before deciding anything, is what makes a resolution feel fair to everyone. For example, if two teammates disagree about how to split credit for a project, hearing both people's full explanation before suggesting a solution makes the eventual decision feel much fairer to both.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two teammates disagree about how to split credit. What makes the resolution feel fair?

options.label: Hearing both people's full explanation before deciding
options.outcome: Exactly right! Listening to both sides of a disagreement fully, before deciding anything, is what makes a resolution feel fair to everyone.

options.label: Deciding immediately without hearing both sides
options.outcome: Deciding immediately without hearing both sides can leave one person feeling unheard — listening to both first feels much fairer.

options.label: Fairness in resolving conflict does not matter
options.outcome: Fairness actually matters a lot in resolving conflict — hearing both sides fully is what makes a decision feel fair.

slides.title: Sharing credit
slides.text: A good leader makes sure the whole team gets recognized for a success, not just themselves. For example, if your group project gets praised by a teacher, saying "we all worked hard on this together" instead of taking all the credit yourself is what earns real respect from your teammates.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group project gets praised by a teacher. What earns real respect from teammates?

options.label: "We all worked hard on this together"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good leader makes sure the whole team gets recognized for a success, not just themselves.

options.label: Taking all the credit yourself
options.outcome: Taking all the credit yourself can damage trust with teammates — sharing credit earns real respect instead.

options.label: Sharing credit never matters to a team
options.outcome: Sharing credit actually matters a lot — it's what earns real respect from teammates.

slides.title: Handling setbacks
slides.text: How a leader reacts right after something goes wrong often decides whether the team panics or keeps working. For example, if a project's code crashes the night before a deadline, a leader who calmly says "let's figure out the fix together" keeps the team focused instead of scared.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your team's project idea completely fails during testing, right before the deadline. What's the best leadership response?

options.label: Stay calm, regroup the team, and figure out the next step together
options.outcome: Exactly — staying composed and leading the team through the setback (instead of panicking) is what good leaders do when plans fall apart.

options.label: Panic and blame whoever's idea it was
options.outcome: Panicking and blaming makes the team more anxious and less focused on actually solving the problem.

options.label: Give up on the project entirely
options.outcome: A setback doesn't mean the project is over — regrouping and adjusting the plan is usually possible, even close to a deadline.

slides.title: Breaking a vision into steps
slides.text: Having a clear goal isn't enough on its own; a good leader also breaks it into smaller steps the team can actually act on. For example, "every judge remembers our project" becomes concrete once it's broken into steps like "make one unforgettable visual" and "practice our opening line until it's smooth."

widgetConfig.scenario: Your goal is 'every judge remembers our project.' What makes this goal actionable?

options.label: Breaking it into steps like "make one unforgettable visual"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Having a clear goal isn't enough on its own — breaking it into smaller, actionable steps is what a good leader does too.

options.label: Just repeating the big vague goal
options.outcome: Repeating the big vague goal doesn't make it actionable — breaking it into concrete steps does.

options.label: Breaking goals into steps never helps
options.outcome: Breaking goals into steps actually helps a lot — it turns a vague vision into something the team can actually act on.

slides.title: Staying calm when plans change
slides.text: Unexpected changes are common, and a leader's calm reaction helps the team adjust instead of panicking. For example, if the venue for a presentation changes the day before, a leader who says "let's figure out what's different and adjust" keeps the whole team steady.

widgetConfig.scenario: The venue for your presentation changes the day before. What helps the team most?

options.label: "Let's figure out what's different and adjust"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Unexpected changes are common, and a leader's calm reaction helps the team adjust instead of panicking.

options.label: Panicking in front of the team
options.outcome: Panicking in front of the team can spread anxiety — staying calm helps everyone adjust much better.

options.label: A leader's calm reaction never affects the team
options.outcome: A leader's calm reaction actually affects the team a lot — it keeps everyone steady during unexpected changes.

slides.title: Finding a compromise both sides can accept
slides.text: After hearing both sides of a disagreement, a good leader looks for a solution that gives each side something, rather than simply picking one side as the winner. For example, if two teammates disagree about the project's color scheme, using both colors in different sections can satisfy both of them.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two teammates disagree about which project idea to use. What should a good leader try to do?

options.label: Find a solution that gives both sides something they value
options.outcome: Exactly! A good compromise gives each side something meaningful, rather than one side winning completely.

options.label: Just pick whichever side argued louder
options.outcome: Picking based on volume isn't fair — a good leader looks for a solution both sides can accept.

options.label: Avoid making any decision at all
options.outcome: Avoiding the decision doesn't resolve the disagreement — a good leader works toward a fair compromise.

slides.title: Learning from a setback
slides.text: After something goes wrong, a good leader takes time to figure out what to do differently next time, not just to move past it quickly. For example, after a presentation that didn't go well, a leader who asks "what would we change if we did this again?" helps the team actually improve.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT a good way to respond to a setback?

items.label: Try a new approach next time
Talk about it honestly with the team

widgetConfig.explanation: Blaming a teammate publicly doesn't help anyone learn — the other three are healthy ways to respond to a setback and actually improve next time.

slides.title: Celebrating the team's effort, not just the result
slides.text: Recognizing hard work even when the outcome isn't perfect keeps a team motivated for the next challenge. For example, after a project that didn't win a prize, thanking the team for how hard they worked keeps everyone willing to try again next time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your project didn't win a prize, but the team worked hard. What keeps everyone motivated?

options.label: Thanking the team for how hard they worked
options.outcome: Exactly right! Recognizing hard work even when the outcome isn't perfect keeps a team motivated for the next challenge.

options.label: Only celebrating if you win
options.outcome: Only celebrating wins can leave a team feeling unappreciated after a loss — recognizing effort keeps them motivated.

options.label: Effort never deserves recognition without a win
options.outcome: Effort actually deserves recognition even without a win — it's what keeps a team motivated to try again.

quiz.question: Two teammates disagree about splitting credit. What makes the resolution feel fair?
choices: Both sides being fully heard first
Deciding quickly without hearing anyone out
quiz.explanation: Hearing both people's full explanation before deciding anything is what makes a resolution actually feel fair. If you decide quickly without listening, at least one side is left feeling ignored, even if the final decision was reasonable.

quiz.question: Your group project gets praised. Why say "we all worked hard" instead of taking credit alone?
choices: Everyone contributed and deserves recognition
The leader should always get the credit
quiz.explanation: Saying "we all worked hard on this" recognizes that a success usually comes from the whole team's effort, not just the leader's. Taking all the credit alone, even without meaning to, can make teammates feel unseen and less willing to contribute next time.

quiz.question: Saying "we want every judge to remember our project by name" instead of "let's do our best" is an example of what?
choices: Setting a clear vision
Giving vague instructions
quiz.explanation: A clear vision, like "every judge remembers our project by name," gives a team something specific to work toward. A vague goal like "let's do our best" doesn't tell anyone what success would actually look like.

quiz.question: Project code crashes the night before a deadline. What should a leader do?
choices: Calmly say let's figure out the fix together
Panic and blame whoever wrote the code
quiz.explanation: How a leader reacts right after something goes wrong often decides whether the team panics or keeps working. Calmly saying "let's figure out the fix together" keeps everyone focused instead of scared, even under real pressure.

quiz.question: The goal is "every judge remembers our project." What should a leader do next?
choices: Break it into concrete steps the team can act on
Just repeat the goal and hope it happens
