quiz.explanation: A clear goal isn't useful on its own until it's broken into steps a team can actually act on. Turning "every judge remembers our project" into concrete tasks, like "make one unforgettable visual," gives the team something to actually do.

quiz.question: The presentation venue changes the day before the event. What should a leader do?
choices: Stay calm and figure out what needs to adjust
Panic and blame whoever booked the room
quiz.explanation: Unexpected changes, like a venue switching the day before, are common, and a leader's calm reaction helps the team adjust instead of panicking. Saying "let's figure out what's different" keeps everyone steady and focused on solving the problem.

quiz.question: Two teammates disagree about the project's color scheme. What's a good compromise?
choices: Use both colors in different sections
Only use one person's color and ignore the other
quiz.explanation: After hearing both sides of a disagreement, a good leader looks for a solution that gives each side something instead of just picking a winner. Using both colors in different sections, instead of choosing only one, can satisfy both teammates.

quiz.question: A presentation didn't go well. What should a good leader ask afterward?
choices: What would we change if we did this again?
Whose fault was it?
quiz.explanation: Learning from a setback means figuring out what to do differently next time, not just moving on quickly. Asking "what would we change if we did this again?" turns a disappointing result into something the team can actually improve from.

quiz.question: A project doesn't win a prize, but the team worked hard. What should a good leader do?
choices: Thank the team for their effort
Only focus on the disappointing result
quiz.explanation: Recognizing hard work, even when the result isn't perfect, keeps a team motivated to try again. Thanking the team for their effort after a loss matters just as much as celebrating an actual win.

quiz.question: After hearing both teammates explain their view on a disagreement, what should a fair leader do next?
choices: Look for a solution that addresses both concerns
Immediately side with whoever spoke first
quiz.explanation: Once both sides have been heard, a fair leader looks for a solution that addresses both people's concerns instead of automatically siding with whoever spoke first. This is what turns a fair process into a fair outcome.

slides.title: Different leadership styles
slides.text: Some leaders direct closely, others coach, others mostly get out of the way — the best style often depends on the team and the situation, not one fixed approach. For example, a brand-new team member might need close, direct guidance at first, while an experienced teammate often does better with a leader who mostly steps back and trusts their judgment.

widgetConfig.scenario: Some leaders direct closely, others coach, others step back and let the team lead itself. Is there only one correct leadership style?

options.label: No — different styles can work well depending on the situation
options.outcome: Exactly right! Different leadership styles — directing, coaching, or stepping back — can each work well depending on the situation.

options.label: Yes, only one leadership style ever works
options.outcome: There isn't just one correct style — different situations call for different leadership approaches.

options.label: Leadership style never matters at all
options.outcome: Leadership style actually matters a lot — choosing the right one for the situation makes a real difference.

slides.title: Servant leadership
slides.text: This style puts the team's needs first, asking "how can I help you succeed?" rather than "how can you help me look good?" For example, a club president practicing servant leadership might spend their time helping members get resources they need for their own projects, rather than mainly focusing on projects that make the president look good.

widgetConfig.scenario: A leadership style asks 'how can I help you succeed?' and puts the team's needs first. What is this style called?

options.label: Servant leadership
options.outcome: Exactly right! Servant leadership puts the team's needs first, asking 'how can I help you succeed?'

options.label: Micromanagement
options.outcome: Micromanagement means controlling every small detail — putting the team's needs first is called servant leadership.

options.label: Authoritarian leadership
options.outcome: Authoritarian leadership is about strict top-down control — asking how to help the team succeed is servant leadership.

slides.title: Delegation vs. micromanaging
slides.text: Genuine delegation means trusting someone with real ownership of a task, instead of micromanaging — assigning the job but then controlling every detail anyway. For example, delegating the social media for a club event means letting that person actually make creative decisions, rather than assigning it to them and then rewriting every post yourself, which is really micromanaging in disguise.

widgetConfig.scenario: You delegated a task to a capable teammate, but you keep checking in every 10 minutes and redoing small parts of their work. What's happening?

options.label: You're micromanaging — true delegation means trusting them to do it their way
options.outcome: Right — delegation means handing off real ownership, not just the task while you still control every detail. Micromanaging undermines the trust delegation is supposed to build.

options.label: That's just normal, careful delegation
options.outcome: Constant check-ins and redoing their work is actually the opposite of delegation — it signals you don't really trust them with it.

options.label: It doesn't matter as long as the work gets done well
options.outcome: It does matter — micromanaging can frustrate capable teammates and prevent them from growing into the role.

slides.title: Leading by example
slides.text: Teams take their real cues from what a leader does, not just what they say — showing up prepared and doing unglamorous work yourself sets the standard everyone else follows. For example, a team captain who stays late to help clean up gear, without being asked, sends a stronger message about effort than any speech about hard work ever could.

widgetConfig.scenario: A team captain stays late to help clean up gear without being asked. What message does this send?

options.label: A stronger message about effort than any speech could
options.outcome: Exactly right! Teams take their real cues from what a leader does, not just what they say — this sends a stronger message than any speech.

options.label: No real message at all
options.outcome: It actually sends a strong message — teams notice what a leader does far more than what they say.

options.label: Actions never speak louder than words for a leader
options.outcome: Actions actually do speak louder than words for a leader — teams take their real cues from what you do.

slides.title: Leading with integrity
slides.text: Making the same ethical choice whether or not anyone's watching is what actually earns long-term respect from a team. For example, giving honest credit for an idea even when nobody would have noticed if you'd taken it for yourself is exactly the kind of consistent integrity that earns lasting trust.

widgetConfig.scenario: You could take credit for an idea that wasn't yours, and nobody would notice. What earns long-term respect?

options.label: Giving honest credit even when nobody would notice
options.outcome: Exactly right! Making the same ethical choice whether or not anyone's watching is what actually earns long-term respect from a team.

options.label: Taking the credit since nobody would know
options.outcome: Taking credit you don't deserve, even secretly, undermines the integrity that earns long-term respect.

options.label: Integrity only matters when someone is watching
options.outcome: Integrity actually matters most when nobody's watching — that consistency is exactly what earns lasting respect.

slides.title: Authority vs. influence
slides.text: Formal authority, like being the captain, and real influence, earned through respect, are not the same thing, and the best leaders build influence rather than relying on their title alone. For example, a co-captain who people actually listen to earned that influence through consistent good judgment, not just the title on the roster.

widgetConfig.scenario: A manager has official authority over their team, but the team doesn't respect or trust them. What's missing?

options.label: Real influence — authority alone doesn't guarantee people genuinely follow
options.outcome: Exactly — having an official title gives you authority, but true leadership influence comes from earning trust and respect, not just the position itself.

options.label: Nothing, authority is all that matters
options.outcome: Authority gives formal power, but without real influence (trust and respect), people may comply reluctantly rather than truly follow.

options.label: More official power would fix it
options.outcome: More authority without building real trust and respect usually doesn't fix the underlying issue — influence has to be earned.

slides.title: The cost of over-delegating
slides.text: Delegating too much, too fast, without checking in, can leave a team member overwhelmed or a project unsupervised, so effective delegation includes staying appropriately available. For example, handing an entire fundraiser off to a new member with zero check-ins can set them up to fail, even though the intention was to trust them.

widgetConfig.scenario: You hand an entire fundraiser to a new member with zero check-ins. What's the risk?

options.label: They could be set up to fail without support
options.outcome: Exactly right! Delegating too much, too fast, without checking in can leave a team member overwhelmed or a project unsupervised.

options.label: Nothing — delegating fully is always the best move
options.outcome: Delegating fully with zero support can actually set someone up to fail — staying appropriately available matters too.

options.label: Checking in with new members never helps
options.outcome: Checking in with new members actually helps a lot — it prevents them from feeling overwhelmed or unsupported.

slides.title: Leading under pressure
slides.text: How a leader behaves when stakes are high and time is short reveals more about their real character than how they act when everything is going smoothly. For example, a leader who stays organized and communicative during a chaotic last-minute event change shows the composure that defines real leadership.

widgetConfig.scenario: A last-minute event change causes chaos. What reveals real leadership?

options.label: Staying organized and communicative under pressure
options.outcome: Exactly right! How a leader behaves when stakes are high and time is short reveals more about their real character than when things are calm.

options.label: Panicking along with everyone else
options.outcome: Panicking along with everyone else doesn't show composure — staying organized under pressure is what reveals real leadership.

options.label: How a leader acts under pressure never matters
options.outcome: How a leader acts under pressure actually matters a lot — it reveals their real character more than calm moments do.

slides.title: Adapting your communication style
slides.text: Explaining the same idea differently depending on who's listening — more detail for someone new, a quick summary for an experienced teammate — is a sign of a thoughtful leader, not inconsistency. For example, walking a first-time volunteer through every step of an event while just briefly confirming the plan with a veteran organizer respects both people's needs.

widgetConfig.scenario: You explain an event step-by-step to a first-time volunteer, but just briefly confirm the plan with a veteran. Is this inconsistent?

options.label: No — adapting your explanation to each person is thoughtful, not inconsistent
options.outcome: Exactly right! Explaining the same idea differently depending on who's listening is a sign of a thoughtful leader, not inconsistency.

options.label: Yes, you should explain things identically to everyone
options.outcome: Explaining things identically to everyone ignores what each person actually needs — adapting is more thoughtful, not inconsistent.

options.label: Communication style never needs to change for different people
options.outcome: Communication style actually should change for different people — it respects both the newcomer's and the veteran's needs.

quiz.question: A brand-new team member needs close guidance, while an experienced one does better with more independence. What does this show?
choices: No single leadership style is correct for every situation
Yes, one style always works best
quiz.explanation: Effective leadership isn't one fixed style — it adapts to the person and situation. A brand-new teammate often needs close, direct guidance to get started, while an experienced one usually performs better when a leader steps back and trusts their judgment.

quiz.question: What does "servant leadership" prioritize?
choices: The team's needs and success
Making the leader look good
quiz.explanation: Servant leadership is a style where the leader's main job is supporting the team's success, not their own image. A club president practicing it spends time helping members get what they need for their own projects, rather than chasing recognition for themselves.

quiz.question: Delegating social media but then rewriting every post yourself — what's actually happening?
choices: Micromanaging, not genuine delegation
True delegation with real ownership
quiz.explanation: Genuine delegation means trusting someone with real ownership of a task's decisions, not just its labor. Assigning social media to a teammate and then rewriting every post yourself is really micromanaging — controlling the details while pretending to have let go.

quiz.question: Giving honest credit for an idea even when nobody would have noticed otherwise. What does this show?
choices: Leading with integrity — the same choice whether or not anyone's watching
Only acting ethically when being observed
quiz.explanation: Leading with integrity means making the same ethical choice whether or not anyone is watching. Giving honest credit for an idea, even when nobody would have noticed if you'd taken it yourself, is exactly the kind of consistency that earns lasting respect.

quiz.question: A team captain stays late to help clean up gear without being asked. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Leading by example
Delegating unpleasant tasks to others
quiz.explanation: Teams take their real cues from what a leader actually does, not just what they say. A captain who stays late to help clean up gear, without being asked, sends a far stronger message about effort than any speech about hard work could.

quiz.question: A co-captain has real influence on the team even though they don't have the official title. What does this show?
choices: Influence is earned through respect, not just given by title
Only official titles create real influence
quiz.explanation: Formal authority — the power that comes with an official title — is different from influence, which is earned through consistent good judgment and respect. A co-captain people actually listen to has usually built that influence over time, not just been handed it.

quiz.question: A leader hands off an entire fundraiser to a brand-new member with zero check-ins. What's the risk?
choices: Over-delegating without support can set someone up to fail
There's no downside to delegating everything at once
quiz.explanation: Delegating too much, too fast, without staying available, can leave someone overwhelmed and a project quietly unsupervised. Handing an entire fundraiser to a new member with zero check-ins can set them up to fail, even though the intention was to trust them.

quiz.question: An event's plans change chaotically at the last minute. What reveals a leader's real character?
choices: Staying organized and communicative under pressure
Only how they act when things go smoothly
quiz.explanation: How a leader behaves when stakes are high and time is short reveals more about their real character than how they act when things are calm. Staying organized and communicative during a chaotic last-minute change shows the kind of composure that actually defines good leadership.

quiz.question: A leader explains an event in full detail to a first-time volunteer, but just confirms the plan briefly with a veteran. What is this?
choices: Thoughtfully adapting communication to the listener
Being inconsistent and unfair
quiz.explanation: Explaining an idea differently depending on who's listening — more detail for someone new, a quick summary for an experienced teammate — is thoughtful adaptation, not inconsistency. Walking a first-time volunteer through every step while briefly confirming a plan with a veteran respects both people's actual needs.

quiz.question: A new leader wants people to follow safety rules at an event. What is the most effective way to make that happen?
choices: Follow the rules themselves first
Just announce the rules and not follow them personally
quiz.explanation: The most effective way to get people to follow rules is to follow them yourself first, since teams copy what a leader actually does far more than what they say. A leader who skips their own safety rules undermines the message no matter how firmly they announce it.

slides.title: Leading through team conflict
slides.text: A strong leader acts as a fair facilitator during conflict, not a judge picking sides, helping the team find its own resolution. For example, if two club members clash over how to run an event, a strong leader might guide a conversation where both explain their view and propose their own compromise, rather than the leader simply declaring a winner.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two club members clash over how to run an event. What does a strong leader do?

options.label: Guide a conversation where both propose a compromise
options.outcome: Exactly right! A strong leader acts as a fair facilitator during conflict, not a judge picking sides, helping the team find its own resolution.

options.label: Declare a winner themselves
options.outcome: Declaring a winner themselves acts like a judge picking sides — guiding both sides to a compromise works much better.

options.label: A leader should never get involved in conflict
options.outcome: A leader actually should get involved, as a fair facilitator helping both sides find their own resolution.

slides.title: Emotional intelligence in leadership
slides.text: Noticing how team members are feeling, not just what they're doing, often prevents problems before they even start. For example, noticing a normally engaged teammate has become unusually quiet in meetings, and checking in privately, can catch a brewing problem — burnout, a personal issue, a disagreement — before it affects the whole team's work.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teammate seems unusually quiet and withdrawn during a meeting. What does emotionally intelligent leadership look like here?

options.label: Notice the change and check in privately with genuine concern
options.outcome: Exactly — emotional intelligence means noticing subtle emotional cues and responding with genuine care, not just focusing on tasks.

options.label: Ignore it since it's not about the work
options.outcome: Ignoring emotional cues can miss something important affecting the team — noticing and checking in shows real emotional intelligence.

options.label: Call them out in front of the group for being quiet
options.outcome: Calling someone out publicly about something personal can feel embarrassing — a private, caring check-in works much better.

slides.title: Creating space to be heard
slides.text: A leader who actively invites disagreement, and doesn't punish people for raising concerns, builds what's sometimes called psychological safety — a team where people feel safe speaking up. For example, asking "does anyone see a problem with this plan?" and genuinely welcoming the answer, even if it's critical, makes a team far more likely to catch mistakes early.

widgetConfig.scenario: You ask 'does anyone see a problem with this plan?' and genuinely welcome critical answers. What does this build?

options.label: A team that feels safe speaking up
options.outcome: Exactly right! A leader who actively invites disagreement without punishing it builds what's called psychological safety.

options.label: A team that is afraid to disagree
options.outcome: Genuinely welcoming critical answers builds the opposite — a team that feels safe speaking up, not afraid to disagree.

options.label: Inviting disagreement never helps catch mistakes
options.outcome: Inviting disagreement actually helps catch mistakes early — it makes a team far more likely to speak up before problems grow.

slides.title: Giving credit publicly and specifically
slides.text: Naming exactly who did what well, and doing it where others can hear, builds far more trust than a vague "great job, team." For example, saying "Priya's research is the reason our argument held up under questioning" in front of the whole group recognizes a specific contribution in a way generic praise never does.

widgetConfig.scenario: Which builds more trust: a vague 'great job, team' or naming a specific contribution?

options.label: Naming a specific contribution, like whose research held up under questioning
options.outcome: Exactly right! Naming exactly who did what well, where others can hear it, builds far more trust than a vague 'great job, team.'

options.label: A vague "great job, team" works just as well
options.outcome: A vague comment doesn't recognize anyone's specific contribution the way naming it directly does — specificity builds more trust.

options.label: Public credit never builds more trust than private
options.outcome: Public, specific credit actually builds more trust than a vague comment, by recognizing exactly what someone contributed.

slides.title: Owning mistakes publicly
slides.text: A leader who admits their own errors openly, instead of quietly fixing them or shifting blame, gives the whole team permission to be honest about mistakes too. For example, telling a team "I misjudged how long this would take, that's on me, here's the new plan" models the same honesty a leader expects from everyone else.

widgetConfig.scenario: As the team lead, you made a decision that turned out to hurt the project's progress. What's the best way to handle it?

options.label: Own the mistake openly with the team and explain the fix
options.outcome: That's strong leadership — owning mistakes openly builds trust and shows the team it's safe to take risks and be honest too.

options.label: Quietly fix it without mentioning it was your call
options.outcome: Hiding the mistake might feel safer, but it can erode trust if the team finds out later — and it misses a chance to model accountability.

options.label: Let the team think it was someone else's decision
options.outcome: Shifting blame damages trust badly when it comes out — real leaders own their decisions, good and bad.

slides.title: Reading the room
slides.text: Noticing the overall mood of a group — tension, fatigue, excitement — before deciding how to run a meeting is a skill that separates good leaders from great ones. For example, sensing that a team is exhausted after a long week might mean shortening a meeting rather than pushing through a full agenda.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your team seems exhausted after a long week. What should a good leader consider?
